preamble: Vocalization of the voiced velar fricative [ɣ] to the labio-velar approximant [w] after back vowels. The friction is lost while the velar gesture remains and lip rounding is added from the preceding vowel. It happened in Early Middle English, where post-vocalic Old English [ɣ] produced new aw/ow diphthongs (lagu > lawe 'law'); in Danish, where older post-vocalic [ɣ] became [w] after back vowels and /r/ (Old Danish skogh > skov [ˈsɡ̊ɒwˀ]); and in the Kipchak Turkic languages, where syllable-final Proto-Turkic *g, [ɣ] after back vowels (Old Turkic taɣ), became w (Tatar, Kazakh, Bashkir taw 'mountain').

examples.note: Old English post-vocalic /g/ was [ɣ] between voiced sounds. In Early Middle English it vocalized to [w] after back vowels, creating new aw/ow diphthongs.
The same vocalization gives the ow diphthong of modern bow (weapon).
Older Standard Danish had a distinctive [ɣ], which corresponds to [w] after back vowels and /r/ (and to /j/ after front vowels) in the modern standard language.
The modern spelling ⟨v⟩ stands for the [w] reflex.
Syllable-final *g, realized [ɣ] after back vowels, became w across Kipchak: Tatar and Bashkir тау taw, Karakalpak taw. Oghuz kept the velar (Turkish dağ).
Bashkir has the same form бау baw.
